transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump will have one-on-one meetings with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir
Putin in addition to a joint meeting with all three leaders together during an economic
forum in China.
NPR's Deepa Shivram reports it'll be the first time that's ever happened.
It's Trump's last day of his whirlwind trip to Asia, stopping first in the Philippines
for a regional summit then arriving in Shenzhen, China.
The focus of his highly-watched meeting with Xi in Putin is supposed to be about denuclearization,
though the White House has already said they're not expecting this discussion to produce any
agreement to decrease the number of nuclear weapons.
Even if there are no deliverables from the meeting, Trump will get the photo op moment
as he tries to cement his legacy on the world stage in his last two years in office.
Deepa Shivram, NPR News, Shenzhen.
A slew of recent digital service disruptions affecting everything from Microsoft Outlook
to flight communications are wreaking havoc across the Internet, but experts tell NPR's
Jenna McLaughlin that there's no evidence cyberattacks are to blame.
The National Security Agency financial executives and others have told Congress that a series
of recent service outages affecting the NSA's classified networks, banking applications
and other digital services are the result of technical glitches caused by a large volume
of critical updates to systems.
It's according to a congressional source not authorized to speak on the record.
With the advent of artificial intelligence, it's becoming easier and faster to find vulnerabilities
in systems.
Companies are being forced to rapidly patch those holes to prevent attacks, but sometimes
those patches are difficult to apply or cause unintended disruptions.
Cybersecurity experts tell NPR the Internet has always been fragile, and the industry
is still adjusting to the pace of updates in the age of AI.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
In Los Angeles, jurors are deliberating after hearing closing arguments in the retrial of
the man accused of setting a fire that eventually became last year's deadly Palisades Fire,
Steve Futterman reports.
In closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Jonathan Rinderknecht was angry when
he allegedly started the Lachman Fire just past midnight on New Year's Day last year.
That fire, they claim, was never completely put out and reemerged a week later as the
Palisades Fire, which killed a dozen people and destroyed thousands of homes.
Defense Attorney Steve Haney argued that the fire was started by New Year's celebrants
setting off fireworks.
It occurred right around midnight on New Year's, when that's one of the most active times for
fireworks in America, so it's a logical inference.
In the first trial, jurors were split 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman at the Federal Courthouse in Los Angeles.
AI company Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 per share ahead of
its debut on Wall Street tomorrow.
It's above the expected price range and values the maker of clawed AI at $1.5 trillion.
It comes at a moment when investors are nervous of an AI boom overly reliant on debt.
This is NPR News.
A federal judge has temporarily extended for two weeks an order blocking the Trump administration
from breaking ground on a towering arch in the nation's capital.
It was due to expire tomorrow.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he
remakes the landscape of Washington, D.C.
Older Americans are among the millions who've lost SNAP food benefits since Republican lawmakers
passed sweeping changes to the program.
And here's Jennifer Ludden reports.
Lisa Reese stopped working at 62 to help out family, including taking care of a granddaughter
to save on daycare costs, but she could barely get by as prices shot up this year, especially
her gas bill.
Oh, my goodness.
That went through the roof.
One of my bills was $500.
This summer, she was approved for $63 a month in food aid.
But to get it under new work rules, she volunteers 80 hours a month at a local food pantry.
The Trump administration says such requirements are cutting costs and tackling fraud.
Reese loves helping out, but...
I have arthritis in my hand real bad, high blood pressure, you name it.
She's not sure how long she can keep it up.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Capitol Heights, Maryland.
During President Trump's visit to the Philippines, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. says he sent
a delivery of jollibee fried rice, fried chicken, rather, to President Trump so he could have
a taste of Manila.
Jollibee is a popular local fast food chain that's known for its fried chicken.
It's also become a feature of regional diplomacy, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese
visited a jollibee branch in Manila this week.
I'm Rylan Barton.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from Angie.
Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros to get their home projects done well
for over 30 years.
For everything from minor repairs to major remodels, find reviews, pricing and booking
at angie.com or on the Angie app.

topics.text: Trump to hold one-on-one meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin during Shenzhen trip
Digital service outages across Microsoft Outlook and flight communications attributed to technical glitches, not cyberattacks
Jury deliberates retrial of Jonathan Rinderknecht, accused of starting fire that became Palisades Fire
Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, valuing AI company at $1.5 trillion
Federal judge extends two-week block on Trump administration's towering arch construction in Washington
Older Americans losing SNAP benefits under new work requirements, such as Lisa Reese's volunteer hours
Marcos sends Jollibee fried chicken to Trump during Philippines visit
